title: India's Largest Mutual Fund House Is Going Public — and Abu Dhabi and Singapore's Sovereign Funds Are Already In
excerpt: SBI Funds Management's $1.2 billion IPO kicks off a wave of blockbuster listings that could raise $50 billion in the second half of 2026.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • SBI Funds Management's IPO aims to raise $1.2 billion, attracting major sovereign funds.
  • The IPO is part of a larger trend, with 251 companies seeking $51.7 billion in funding.
  • SBI Funds manages $131.1 billion in assets, holding over 15% of India's mutual fund market.
  • Institutional demand for the IPO is nearly five times the reserved amount, with 50% for retail investors.
  • Foreign portfolio investors are returning, with significant inflows into Indian banking stocks.

India's largest mutual fund house is about to go public, and some of the world's biggest money is lining up to get in. SBI Funds Management, the joint venture between State Bank of India and France's Amundi, will draw cornerstone investments from Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) and Singapore's GIC in a $1.2 billion initial public offering that is expected to open next week. The listing marks the most significant IPO India has seen since early 2026, when rising oil prices linked to the Iran conflict dampened market sentiment and stalled the country's once-booming primary market. It also signals a broader revival: 251 companies are now waiting in the pipeline to raise a combined ₹4.93 lakh crore ($51.7 billion), according to PRIME Database. ## What SBI Funds Management Brings to Market SBI Funds Management is not a startup looking for validation. It manages ₹12.5 lakh crore ($131.1 billion) in assets as of March 2026, commanding more than 15 percent of India's mutual fund market. The company reported a net profit of ₹2,531 crore in FY25, up from ₹2,062 crore the year before. The IPO is structured as a pure offer-for-sale: SBI will sell 6.3 percent and Amundi will sell 3.7 percent of their holdings. No new shares will be issued, meaning all proceeds go to existing shareholders. The company is expected to be valued at around $12.3 billion — comparable to rival ICICI Prudential Asset Management, which is valued at roughly $17.6 billion following its own December listing. Institutional demand has been extraordinary. Sources with direct knowledge of the deal told Reuters that commitments from institutional investors already stand at nearly five times the amount reserved for them. Despite this, the fund house plans to keep 50 percent of the offering available to individual investors — an unusually democratic allocation for an IPO of this size. ## Why Sovereign Wealth Funds Are Betting Big The participation of ADIA and GIC is not incidental. Both sovereign wealth funds have been steadily increasing their exposure to India's financial services sector, which benefits from a rare combination: a large and growing domestic savings pool, rising financial literacy, a young population, and a regulatory environment that has matured considerably under SEBI. > **""My sense is that the worst of the FPI selling is over and outflows will reduce significantly," said Abhay Laijawala, chief investment officer for India at Lighthouse Canton."** India's mutual fund industry has nearly tripled in assets under management over the past five years, driven by the SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) revolution that has brought millions of first-time retail investors into the market. Monthly SIP inflows now exceed ₹25,000 crore, providing Indian equity markets with a structural domestic bid that partly insulates them from foreign portfolio investor volatility. For global investors, SBI Funds offers a proxy for this entire growth story — without the direct equity market risk that comes with buying individual Indian stocks. ## The Broader IPO Revival ![Abu Dhabi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg/3840px-Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg) The SBI Funds listing does not exist in isolation. It is the first in a wave of large offerings that could reshape India's public markets in the second half of 2026. Manipal Health Enterprises has already received SEBI approval for a $1.2 billion healthcare IPO. Indo-MIM, the world's largest metal injection moulding company, is planning a $471 million offering. And the two mega-listings everyone is watching — the National Stock Exchange of India (estimated at $3.3 billion) and Reliance Jio ($3.8 billion) — are both expected before year-end. "While the big-name IPOs that are potentially lined up for this month have good traction, the kind of response they receive and listing will determine the fate of the other bigger issues in the pipeline," Suraj Krishnaswamy, managing director at Axis Capital, told Reuters.

## Foreign Money Is Coming Back The IPO wave coincides with a measurable shift in foreign investor sentiment toward India. After record outflows of $29 billion from Indian equities earlier in 2026, foreign portfolio investors turned net buyers in the second half of June, pouring ₹146.34 billion ($1.54 billion) into banking stocks alone — the highest fortnightly inflow in 14 months. Several policy moves are fuelling this reversal. In June, the Reserve Bank of India extended a subsidised forex swap facility for lenders' overseas borrowings and allowed banks to lend to non-residents against foreign currency deposits. The government scrapped capital gains tax on FPI investments in government securities and removed the 20 percent withholding tax on interest income, effective April 1. The Nifty Bank index gained 6.1 percent in June, leading the broader Nifty 50's 1.4 percent rise. HDFC Bank alone climbed 7.2 percent after clearing a corporate governance review. "My sense is that the worst of the FPI selling is over and outflows will reduce significantly," said Abhay Laijawala, chief investment officer for India at Lighthouse Canton. ## What NRI Investors Should Know For diaspora investors, the SBI Funds IPO presents both an opportunity and a reminder. The opportunity is straightforward: SBI Mutual Fund is the brand most Indian households associate with trusted, government-backed investing. Its parent, SBI, is the country's largest bank by assets. Owning shares in the company that manages India's largest pool of retail savings is a direct bet on India's financialisation — the long-term shift from gold and real estate to equities and mutual funds.

The reminder is about access. NRIs can participate in Indian IPOs, but the process requires an active demat account with an Indian brokerage, PAN card verification, and compliance with FEMA regulations. Those with existing SIPs through SBI Mutual Fund should note that the IPO listing will not directly affect their fund holdings — they are buying shares in the fund management company, not units in the funds it manages. With 50 percent of the offering reserved for individual investors and the broader market signalling a return of foreign confidence, this may be the most accessible entry point for NRIs looking to add India's financial sector to their portfolios since the market correction earlier this year.
